extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (TC 3600), patent prosecution attorneys and staff applying KSR obviousness principles
extracted.subtask_description: Training guidance for applying KSR and the Graham factual inquiries to determine obviousness rejections in the examination of business-method-related patent claims. Presents seven distinct rationales (A–G) with the specific findings an examiner must articulate and illustrated examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries (scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims, level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations) before applying any obviousness rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement appears at the start of each rationale: examiners must identify the relevant Graham findings and then—based on those facts—make additional findings specific to the chosen KSR rationale. Additional factual findings beyond the numbered rationale items may be necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale A — Combining Prior Art Elements According To Known Methods to Yield Predictable Results
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the prior art included each element claimed, although not necessarily in a single prior art reference, with the only difference between the claimed invention and the prior art being the lack of actual combination of the elements in a single prior art reference; (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods and that in combination, each element merely would have performed the same function as it did separately; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/example: The rationale supports obviousness where all claimed elements are known in the prior art and their combination would yield only predictable results. Examiners should identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill to combine the elements. If any required finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. Example provided: online remote banking system (claim elements found across Jones and Smith); examiner showed each element in prior art, combination by known methods, predictability of result, and issued a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (Jones in view of Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale B — Simple Substitution of One Known Element for Another to Obtain Predictable Results
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device (method, product, etc.) which differed from the claimed device by the substitution of some components (steps, elements, etc.) with other components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have substituted one known element for another, and the results of the substitution would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/example: Obviousness can be shown by replacing a known component with another known component that performs the same function predictably. Example: substituting bioauthentication (fingerprint sensor) for a PIN in a consumer electronics device—primary reference showed sub-credit/PIN structure, secondary references showed bioauthentication; substitution was predictable and rendered the claim obvious (ex parte Catan example). Examiners should identify each element and confirm the substituted element and its known function in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale C — Use of Known Techniques to Improve Similar Devices (Methods, or Products) in the Same Way
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an 'improvement'; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a 'comparable' device (method, or product that are not the same as the base device) that was improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have applied the known 'improvement' technique in the same way to the 'base' device (method, or product) and the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/example: This rationale applies when a known improvement technique taught in one context would predictably improve a base device in a similar way. The Supreme Court in KSR warns that if the application would have been beyond ordinary skill, the rationale is inappropriate. Example: adding biometric+smart-card authentication and validation form (Wells) to a base remote-transfer system (Barnes) to achieve improved security—predictable adaptation supports a 103 rejection (Barnes in view of Wells). Examiners should identify base and comparable devices and show predictable application of the improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D — Applying a Known Technique to a Known Device Ready for Improvement to Yield Predictable Results
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an 'improvement'; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a known technique that is applicable to the base device (method, or product); (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results and resulted in an improved system; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/example: Similar to C but emphasizes that the base device was 'ready for improvement' and a known technique could be directly applied with predictable results. Example provided: record-keeping system (Reference A) and data-processing breakdown technique (Reference B) — applying sub-files/category codes to banking records would be a predictable improvement (Reference A in view of Reference B). Examiners should explain readiness for improvement and predictable results, and may cite benefits/advantages to support the motivation to adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E — Obvious To Try: Choosing From a Finite Number of Identified, Predictable Solutions, With a Reasonable Expectation of Success
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that at the time of the invention, there had been a recognized problem or need in the art, which may include a design need or market pressure to solve a problem; (2) a finding that there had been a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions to the recognized need or problem; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/example: 'Obvious to try' supports obviousness where there were a limited set of predictable options and a person of ordinary skill would have pursued them expecting success. Example: online bookstore with e-mail customer surveys—survey methods were a finite set and e-mail was an obvious, predictable choice (Smith in view of John). Examiners should identify the recognized problem, the finite predictable solutions, and the reasonable expectation of success for the selected option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F — Known Work In One Field May Prompt Predictable Variations for Use In Same or Different Field Based On Design Incentives or Market Forces
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the scope and content of the prior art, whether in the same field of the endeavor as that of the applicant's invention or a different field of endeavor, included a similar or analogous device (method, or product); (2) a finding that there were design incentives or market forces which would have prompted adaptation of the known device (method or product); (3) a finding that the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art were encompassed in known variations or in a principle known in the prior art; (4) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art, in view of the design incentives or other market forces, could have implemented the claim variation of the prior art, and the claimed variation would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; and (5) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/example: Applies when adaptation from one field to another (or within the same field) would be predictable in view of market/design incentives. Example: modernizing an electro-mechanical child's toy to electronics (Leapfrog v. Fisher-Price)—applying known electronics to achieve smaller size, reliability, and lower cost was predictable and obvious. Examiners should identify analogous prior art, design incentives, known variations, and predictability of the adaptation; list advantages and show no unpredictable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G — Some Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation (TSM) in the Prior Art to Modify or Combine References
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that there was some teaching, suggestion, or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings; (2) a finding that there was reasonable expectation of success; and (3) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/example: This is the classical TSM approach reconceived in light of KSR—examiners must show motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success. Example (same as Rationale C invention): combining Barnes (remote transfer with validation form) and Wells (smart-card/fingerprint authentication) provided motivation and reasonable expectation of success to create the claimed secure remote transfer method; examiner issued a 103 rejection (Barnes in view of Wells). Examiners should identify motivating teachings or general knowledge and explain why success would have been expected.
